summary: Explains issues with sending RTP data packets and RTCP control packets on a single UDP port, and says when it is and is not appropriate. It updates RFC 3550 and RFC 3551 and describes how SDP can signal it. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Usually a call uses one door for voice and another door for control notes. This document explains when both can share one door, which helps with firewalls.

questions: can rtp and rtcp use the same port

subtitle: How RTP media and RTCP control packets can share one UDP port, and when they should not.

tldr.problem: RTP and RTCP historically use separate UDP ports. With NAT, that means more bindings to maintain, and firewalls need more ports opened.
tldr.mechanism: Both packet kinds are sent to one UDP port and told apart by the RTP payload type and RTCP packet type values. SDP signals the choice with the a=rtcp-mux attribute.
tldr.outcome: Multiplexing is acceptable for unicast sessions, discouraged for Any Source Multicast, and optional in some Source-Specific Multicast flows. It costs some RTP payload type values and can hurt header compression.

today: RFC 5761 is a Proposed Standard. It has been updated by RFC 8035 and RFC 8858, and it updates RFC 3550 and RFC 3551.

sections.title: Why Share a Port
sections.content:
The Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) has two parts: a data transfer protocol and a control protocol, RTCP. Historically they run on separate UDP ports. With wider use of Network Address Port Translation (NAPT), that has become a burden, because keeping several NAT bindings is costly. Firewall administration is harder too, since several ports must be opened for RTP traffic.

RFC 5761 describes how the RTP and RTCP flows for a single media type can run on one port, and when that is appropriate. Mixing several media types, such as audio and video, on one port is not covered. The memo updates Section 11 of RFC 3550, and it also updates RFC 3551.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a shop that needs two separate doors, one for customers and one for deliveries. Guards at the gate find that annoying. This document lets both use the same door.

sections.title: Why the Ports Were Separate
sections.content:
RFC 3550 says the underlying protocol must separate data and control packets, for example by using separate UDP port numbers. The authors list three reasons for leaving this to the transport layer.

  • Simplicity: the RTP implementation does not have to separate data from control packets itself.
  • Efficiency: demultiplexing in one place, by UDP port, is more efficient than splitting it across layers.
  • Third-party monitors: RTCP can be multicast on its own group and port, so a monitor can watch reception quality without seeing the data packets.

These choices suit many uses, but not all. Many RTP deployments do not use IP multicast, and with NAT the transport-layer split now requires complex signalling to open multiple NAT pinholes. The memo therefore offers a single-port alternative, pushing some extra work onto the RTP implementation in exchange for simpler NAT traversal.
sections.plainLanguage: Two doors made the shop simple to run and let an inspector watch only the delivery door. But when the gate guard has to unlock both doors every time, one shared door is easier.

sections.title: Telling RTP and RTCP Apart
sections.content:
On a shared port, the RTCP packet type field sits in the same place as the RTP marker (M) bit plus the RTP payload type (PT). That field can separate the two kinds of packet if two restrictions hold: the RTP payload types in use must differ from the RTCP packet types in use, and for each RTP payload type, PT+128 must also differ from the RTCP packet types in use. The second rule covers an RTP data packet that has its marker bit set.

Some conflicts are already known, listed in the table below. Future RTCP packet types are meant to be assigned in the range 209-223, then 194-199, so that only RTP payload types 64-95 are blocked.

When multiplexing, payload type values in the range 64-95 MUST NOT be used. Dynamic payload types SHOULD be chosen from 96-127 where possible. Values below 64 MAY be used if that is not enough, preferring ones that RFC 3551 does not assign statically.

RTCP packets are normally compound and start with a Sender Report or Receiver Report. The wider ban on payload types is there so that non-compound RTCP packets, allowed in some circumstances by RFC 5506, still work.
sections.plainLanguage: When letters for two different clubs go into one mailbox, each needs a clear stamp so nobody mixes them up. Some stamp numbers are off limits so a letter is never mistaken for the other club's.

sections.title: Signalling with SDP
sections.content:
Multiplexing must be signalled in advance. With the Session Description Protocol (SDP) and the offer/answer model, the media-level attribute a=rtcp-mux carries the request. The initial offer MUST include it. If the answerer wants multiplexing, it MUST include a=rtcp-mux in the answer too, and its payload types MUST follow the Section 4 rules.

If the answer lacks the attribute, the offerer MUST NOT multiplex. It then uses RTCP on a separate port chosen by the usual rules, or signalled with a=rtcp:. This is what happens with a peer that does not understand the attribute. When SDP is used declaratively, the attribute means the sender will multiplex, and the receiver MUST be ready to get RTCP on the RTP port.

Other protocols interact with this:

  • SIP forking: an INVITE can produce several 200 (OK) responses, and some answerers may not support multiplexing. The offerer then listens for RTCP on both the RTP port and the usual RTCP port, and sends RTCP on both.
  • ICE: the offer carries a=rtcp-mux, candidate lines for RTP and RTCP, and an a=rtcp: fallback port. If the answerer agrees, it gives a single RTP candidate, which avoids some connectivity checks.
  • Header compression: RTCP packets mixed into the RTP flow can disturb the patterns that schemes such as ROHC rely on. A classifier that looks only at IP addresses and UDP ports will do badly, so the effect should be considered carefully in some wireless systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sharing a door, both sides must agree. One says "can we share?" and the other says "yes" or stays quiet. If it stays quiet, you keep using two doors.

sections.title: When Multiplexing Is Appropriate
sections.content:
The right choice depends on the kind of session.

  • Unicast: multiplexing is acceptable to ease NAT traversal, provided the payload types follow the Section 4 rules and the multiplexing is signalled in advance.
  • Any Source Multicast (ASM): RTP and RTCP SHOULD NOT be multiplexed. NAT is less of a problem there, and separate ports keep third-party RTCP-only monitors possible.
  • Source-Specific Multicast (SSM): the answer depends on which of three flows is meant. Between media sender and distribution source over an SSM connection, multiplexing MAY be used if signalled. From the distribution source to receivers, it MAY be used, though it may hinder third-party monitors under the simple feedback model. From receivers back to the source the path carries only RTCP, so multiplexing is not a concern.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing a door makes sense for a private call between two people. For a big public event where inspectors watch the control door, keep the doors apart.

sections.title: Bandwidth and Quality of Service
sections.content:
When QoS mechanisms match flows by a three-tuple or five-tuple, the RTCP flow merges with the RTP flow. A reservation must therefore include RTCP bandwidth. On the plus side, RTCP then gets the same treatment as RTP, which gives its statistics more accurate measurements.

Normally the RTP session bandwidth is in the SDP b=AS: or b=TIAS: line, and RTCP is limited to 5% of it. A QoS reservation SHOULD then be made for 105% of the b=AS: value. If a non-standard RTCP fraction is signalled with b=RR: and b=RS:, the reservation SHOULD equal AS + RS + RR, taking RS and RR from the SDP answer.
sections.plainLanguage: If the notes and the voice share one pipe, the pipe must be a little bigger so the notes fit too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not believe multiplexing introduces new security considerations. The known major issues remain the integrity and authentication of the signalling that sets up multiplexing, and the integrity, authentication and confidentiality of the RTP and RTCP traffic. The security considerations of RFC 3550, the RTP profile and the payload formats still apply.

With the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP), multiplexing MUST be done below the SRTP layer. The sender builds SRTP and SRTCP packets with their separate cryptographic contexts and merges them onto one port just before sending. The receiver splits them using the payload type and RTCP packet type rules, and only then does the usual cryptographic processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking the notes and the voice with their own keys still works. You just put them on the same truck at the last moment and sort them again on arrival before opening the locks.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content:
IANA registered one new SDP attribute, rtcp-mux, with the long-form name "RTP and RTCP multiplexed on one port". It is a media-level property attribute and takes no value.

The assignment rules for RTCP control packet types in the RTP Parameters registry also changed. IANA is asked to use unused values from 200-223 where possible, then 194-199, then 1-191 and 224-254. The values 0 and 255 are avoided because all-zeros and all-ones are common in random packets, so avoiding them improves validity checking.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of attributes got one new entry, "rtcp-mux", and new rules for choosing numbers for control-note types so they stay out of the voice numbers' way.
